outcomes: A user builds, tests and serves a workspace in a directory Git does not manage, and every command that needs git history refuses in one line that names git and the command to run
A build in such a directory makes no source claim: its capability packages are stamped with no source binding, and its cached outputs never serve a repository
Inside a repository nothing changes: the same source bindings, the same cache keys, the same project selection
nonGoals: Computing a source binding without Git
Publishing or deploying from a root Git does not manage
Reporting a git failure inside a repository as a missing repository

requirements.text: The scheduler stamps every capability package of a root Git does not manage with an empty sourceBinding, sourceBindingUnavailable true, and its sourceRoot, and asks Git once for the whole closure. A binding that fails inside a repository is stamped empty with the marker unset. Inside a repository the stamp carries the binding Git's enumeration yields. A build at a root Git does not manage, with or without a git program, succeeds, writes its session, and its next identical build hits the local cache.

Every execution cache key of a root Git does not manage carries a sourceState marker; a key computed inside a repository carries none and keeps its address. The two states of one task never share a key, in either direction, and the state reaches every downstream key through the upstream fold. A run's keys and version stamp share one answer to whether Git manages the root, asked at most once, and not when the run's own tree-state capture succeeded. A publication's selection fingerprint carries no marker.
A job command with no target at a root Git does not manage selects every project and says so. A named project needs no Git. Any other git failure still fails the selection with its own message.

At a root Git does not manage, --impacted, --baseline on a job command that names no target, version, and a publish or deploy that executes refuse with exactly one line: what needs git history, whether the git program or the repository is missing, and the command to run. A --baseline beside named projects or --all changes no selection, inside a repository or outside one, so it is not refused. A run that only previews its plan is not refused. A git failure inside a repository keeps its own detail.
